messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 63
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Project Manager
- Trauma Type: Life-threatening illness
- Pcl5: 62

She is 63, a married woman from Oceania who has spent most of her adult life as a project manager, the kind of person who keeps color-coded timelines in her head and calms everyone else when plans start to slip. Before she becomes ill, she is the dependable center of things at work and at home. She manages contractors, budgets, and deadlines with quiet authority, and in her marriage she is the one who remembers birthdays, organizes trips, and makes sure the practical parts of life keep moving. She has always believed that if she stays organized and works hard enough, most crises can be managed.

That belief begins to fracture when she develops what she first assumes is an ordinary health problem. She tells herself she is just tired, just run down, just needing rest. But the symptoms come quickly and then all at once. There are scans, urgent voices, long waits in bright hospital corridors, and then a rush of decisions she can barely absorb. At some point, a doctor explains that her condition is serious and potentially life-threatening. She remembers that moment less as a conversation than as a bodily event: the room narrowing, the doctor’s mouth moving, her husband reaching for her hand while she feels as if she has dropped through the floor.

The weeks that follow are filled with procedures, alarms, and the humiliating vulnerability of needing strangers to help her wash, move, and breathe comfortably. She learns the rhythms of the ward at night, when machines beep and footsteps approach and she cannot tell whether someone is coming to help her or to bring more bad news. She becomes terrified of sleep because waking means having to remember where she is. Her husband sits beside her for long hours, trying to sound steady, and she watches his face for clues he is trying to hide. When he goes home, she feels abandoned even though she knows he has no choice.

During the worst stretch of the illness, she becomes convinced she may die. She does not say this often out loud, but she thinks it constantly. She studies the expressions of nurses, trying to detect urgency. She rehearses practical matters in her mind—passwords, bills, who will contact whom—like she is preparing handover notes for a project she will not live to finish. The loss of control unsettles her more than she expects. She cannot fix anything. She cannot even predict whether the next hour will bring relief or another setback.

She survives, and to the people around her this survival begins to look like a success story. Her body slowly recovers, her lab results improve, and eventually she returns home. But home does not feel like home right away. It feels too quiet, too unmonitored. She lies awake listening to the house and wondering if something inside her body is failing again. Any physical sensation—a flutter in her chest, a wave of fatigue, a change in appetite—can send her into spiraling fear. She checks herself repeatedly, researches symptoms late into the night, and startles when the phone rings, half-expecting another call telling her to come back in.

When she returns to work, she does so in the measured way she approaches any difficult project, with spreadsheets, staged hours, and a plan. Colleagues praise her resilience. She smiles and thanks them, but inside she feels brittle. Meetings are hardest when someone speaks casually about health crises or hospitals; her attention drifts and she is suddenly back under fluorescent lights, hearing monitor alarms. She keeps her camera off in virtual meetings on bad days because she does not trust her face. If an email from a medical provider appears in her inbox, her heart pounds so hard she has to stand up and walk away from her desk.

She notices she is no longer the same kind of project manager. She has trouble tolerating uncertainty, even minor changes in schedule. Delays that once seemed manageable now feel threatening. She becomes more rigid, more exacting, and then ashamed of how sharp she sounds with people. She starts overpreparing for everything. Her husband tells her she does not have to do so much, but she cannot explain that planning has become her way of bargaining with danger. If every detail is covered, maybe nothing catastrophic will happen.

At night, memories return with unwelcome clarity: the smell of antiseptic, the pressure of hospital sheets against her skin, the moment she believed she might not see morning. Sometimes she dreams she is back in the hospital and wakes disoriented, clutching the blankets, her body already braced for bad news. She avoids driving past the medical center when she can. She keeps follow-up appointments because she knows she must, but in the waiting room she becomes tense and watchful, scanning staff faces, unable to sit still.

Her husband sees both how far she has come and how much of her remains caught in that period. She is grateful to be alive, and she says so often. Yet gratitude sits alongside anger, fear, and a private sense that the world has become fundamentally unsafe. She still gets up, goes to work, manages teams, answers emails, cooks dinner, and remembers birthdays. From the outside, her life has resumed. Inside, part of her remains in that hospital room, listening for footsteps in the night.
